analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices directly with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill to let Medicare negotiate lower drug prices died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote, a hearing, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: When Medicare's prescription drug benefit (Part D) was created in 2003, the law included a clause forbidding the federal government from interfering with the private plans' drug purchasing — including a ban on the Secretary of Health and Human Services negotiating prices with drug manufacturers. This bill would delete that ban and give the Secretary the same authority other federal agencies have to negotiate bulk prices. It would also require quarterly reports comparing the government-negotiated prices with what uninsured people pay at a retail pharmacy.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who pay out of pocket for prescription drugs, and taxpayers who help fund Part D, if government negotiation brought prices below what private plans currently obtain.

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the statutory 'noninterference' clause so the Secretary of Health and Human Services could negotiate contracts with manufacturers of drugs covered by Part D, aiming to ensure beneficiaries pay the lowest possible price [S3].

Gives the Secretary negotiating authority 'similar to that of other Federal entities that purchase prescription drugs in bulk,' putting Medicare on the same footing as agencies like the Department of Veterans Affairs, which buy large volumes and negotiate prices [S2].

Requires quarterly public reports comparing government-negotiated Part D drug prices with the prices uninsured individuals are charged at retail pharmacies, creating a running public benchmark of the savings (or lack of them) [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose government-negotiated prices for Medicare's enormous drug volume would likely be lower than the prices private plans negotiate. Insurers and pharmacy benefit managers that run Part D plans could also see the government take a larger role in purchasing.

drawbacks.text: HHS negotiation is not guaranteed to beat private-plan prices: Part D plans and pharmacy benefit managers already negotiate on their own, and a single government negotiator might achieve less than boosters projected. The bill's own quarterly price reports appear designed to test exactly that [S3].

Aggressive government negotiation could push manufacturers to protect revenue in other ways, such as charging more to private-pay customers or dropping drugs from negotiated coverage, shifting costs back to other patients.

Giving a federal agency direct purchasing power over a market of this size concentrates substantial pricing discretion in the executive branch, which supporters of the original 'noninterference' clause argued would eventually slide toward government price-setting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential upside for seniors and taxpayers is large, since Medicare is the country's biggest drug buyer, but the bill is a bet that direct government negotiation would outperform the private plans already doing the negotiating. The honest cost is borne by the pharmaceutical industry, with a smaller risk that negotiation produces narrower drug lists or higher prices for people outside Medicare.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on January 11, 2007, and nothing happened after that — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Arlen Specter, a Republican from Pennsylvania, introduced the bill on January 11, 2007, and delivered remarks on the Senate floor the same day [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, which holds jurisdiction over Medicare; that referral is the last action recorded in the 110th Congress [S5].
The Committee on Finance took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or report — and the Senate never voted on it before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which kept the statutory bar on Medicare negotiating prices intact for the rest of the 110th Congress. Part D plans and pharmacy benefit managers also kept their exclusive role in purchasing. The Senate Finance Committee's inaction was what preserved that arrangement, since the bill never advanced beyond referral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers; Part D plans kept their role

for.name: Sen. Arlen Specter
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, delivered introductory remarks, and sought to move it through the Senate Finance Committee

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on January 11, 2007 and took no further recorded action for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote

sides.party_line_note: The bill crossed party lines on paper — a Republican sponsored a Democratic-favored idea — but no other senator from either party signed on, so no party bloc took a recorded position.

industries.note: The bill would end the statutory 'noninterference' clause that bars the government from negotiating, exposing one of the industry's largest customer relationships to bulk-price bargaining. Keeping the bill dead preserved the status quo in which private plans negotiate without government price pressure.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Private drug plans would keep running Part D, but government negotiation could cut into their role as purchasers and squeeze the margins between negotiated prices and their formulary arrangements. Their gain in the actual outcome was keeping sole purchasing authority.
